inserts.title: Displaced foragers reveal a stored outward vector
paragraphs: Müller and Wehner captured food-carrying ants at the feeding location and released each one in open terrain. Each ant's later course was followed on a 10 m spatial scale. That course was measured against the true geographical direction of the nest and against the course predicted from the ant's recorded outbound trajectory. Its outward walk had been recorded before the ant was captured.

In the two-leg experiments, both legs varied over lengths of 5–10 m and turning angles spanning 0–180°. The plotted experiment used a first leg of 10 m and a second leg of 5 m. Release occurred within one minute of capture, which shortened the time before the directional test. The experiments produced a homing direction for each combination of lengths and angles.

Under natural conditions, landmark guidance and systematic searching remain available as additional mechanisms for locating the nest. Each of these can operate alongside a stored home vector, and neither one replaces the other. Landmark guidance and systematic searching are listed as separate mechanisms, each one an addition to the path integrator.
notes: Displaced foragers reveal a stored outward vector.

Müller and Wehner captured food-carrying ants at the feeding location and released each one in open terrain

The plotted experiment used a first leg of 10 m and a second leg of 5 m. Release occurred within one minute of capture, which shortened the time before the directional test. The experiments produced a homing direction for each combination of lengths and angles.

inserts.title: Screening and painting remove two compass inputs
paragraphs: Screening the sun removed direct solar information from the compass. Ants on this route still erred under the screening. The same two-leg geometry had produced homing errors of about 20° at turning angles near 150° in the earlier test. Screening removed the direct sun's information but left the polarized pattern in place. The polarized skylight pattern was still available to the screened ants.

Painting the dorsal rim of the compound eyes removed access to the specialized polarization-sensitive eye region. Ants with painted eyes also erred on the 10 m and 5 m route, which uses the same two-leg geometry as the screened test. Direct sunlight stayed available to these ants, so the sun cue was not removed.

Restricted sky windows can themselves distort polarization estimates. The authors treated this as a separate source of compass error when they interpreted their homing results, which kept the two sources apart. A narrow channel limits the visible part of the sky, which is one way a sky window becomes restricted.
notes: Screening and painting remove two compass inputs.
Explanation 1.
Screening the sun removed direct solar information from the compass

Ants on this route still erred under the screening. The same two-leg geometry had produced homing errors of about 20° at turning angles near 150° in the earlier test. inserts.title: Stilts and stumps alter the distance per stride
paragraphs: Wittlinger and colleagues trained Cataglyphis fortis to a feeder 10 m from the nest. At the feeder, attached pig bristles lengthened the legs to produce stilts, and shortened legs produced stumps. Food-carrying ants were then tested in a separate channel, after their outward distance had already been learned on normal legs.

The first study of this manipulation appeared in Science in 2006 under the title The Ant Odometer: Stepping on Stilts and Stumps. The later follow-up, published in 2007, added a second level of leg shortening. The 2006 paper's figures show normal legs, stilts and stumps side by side.

The 2007 follow-up tested stumps that differed in which leg region was removed. Its normal-legged group served as the reference for each lengthened and shortened condition. Its figures present the four leg conditions as color-coded search distributions.
notes: Stilts and stumps alter the distance per stride.
Explanation 1.
Wittlinger and colleagues trained Cataglyphis fortis to a feeder 10 m from the nest

At the feeder, attached pig bristles lengthened the legs to produce stilts, and shortened legs produced stumps. Food-carrying ants were then tested in a separate channel, after their outward distance had already been learned on normal legs.
Explanation 2.
The first study of this manipulation appeared in Science in 2006 under the title The Ant Odometer: Stepping on Stilts and Stumps
The later follow-up, published in 2007, added a second level of leg shortening. The 2006 paper's figures show normal legs, stilts and stumps side by side.

inserts.title: Graded shortening tests different leg reductions
paragraphs: Stumps I lacked the distal tarsal segments, whereas stumps II had the distal half of the tibia removed. The stilt group was lengthened with bristles, and normal-legged ants provided the reference for every group. Those leg changes were made at the feeder, after the outward distance had been learned.

All groups had acquired the same 10 m outbound feeder distance before the first test. The expanded experiment placed the normal-legged group at 10.20 m, the stumps-I group at 6.95 m and the stumps-II group at 5.75 m. The stilted group reached 15.30 m.

The video was recorded at 250 frames per second before and after each manipulation. The recorded strides were used to measure stride length and walking speed. Workers of larger size carry longer legs. The recorded strides supplied the stride frequency used in the analysis.

inserts.title: Search width tracks the stride-determined spread
paragraphs: The test channel was divided into 10 cm bins before the search data were analyzed. In the first test, the full width at half maximum was 8.3 m for stilts, 6.0 m for normal legs, 5.2 m for stumps I and 4.1 m for stumps II. The search distributions were then plotted for each leg condition.

Stilts had the widest distribution of the four conditions, and stumps II had the narrowest. The four widths follow the same order as the leg treatments that produced them. Search centers for the same conditions were 15.30 m for stilts and 10.20 m for normal legs. The stump-II searches covered the least ground of the four conditions.

Searches in the first test were measured before any matched training, so these widths describe the initial mismatch. Repeated outbound training changed the distributions in the second test. Those widths are full widths at half maximum, reported in meters.
notes: Search width tracks the stride-determined spread.

inserts.title: Stride frequency and length measured at 20 Hz
paragraphs: Stride frequency and stride length are measured separately in the analysis, and either one can change walking speed. Comparing animals at 20 Hz reduced the effect of unequal movement speeds on the predicted homing distances. The analysis used straight runs without abrupt stops. The analysis compared the leg conditions at 20 Hz, which is 20 cycles per second.

Stride length was expressed relative to the alitrunk, a body-size reference. The high-speed records then linked those relative strides with frequency, including the 20 Hz analysis. The curves for stilts, stumps and normal legs were read at matching frequencies.

The stride-length relationship was established independently of the turning-point measures used to locate each ant's nest search. Stilt ants showed longer strides at matched speeds, and stump ants showed shorter ones. Those measures came from freely walking animals. Each leg condition produced its own frequency-length curve.
notes: Stride frequency and length measured at 20 Hz.

Stride frequency and stride length are measured separately in the analysis, and either one can change walking speed

inserts.title: Accumulated movement signals fit a stride integrator
paragraphs: The 2007 experiment combined a 10 m navigational task with leg-length manipulations. In that experiment the leg conditions were stilts, stumps and normal legs. The 2007 paper's title describes a stride integrator that accounts for both stride length and walking speed.

Stilted animals searched at 15.30 m after a 10 m outbound journey, while shortened-leg animals searched at 5.75 m. The search centers came from the middle value of the initial six turning points. Both values came from searches after the same 10 m outbound run.

After one more outbound walk, the searches for all four leg conditions converged on the correct 10 m distance. Stride length was plotted against walking speed in millimeters per second, and the kinematic analysis measured both for each animal.

inserts.title: Lateral-complex synapses respond to light exposure
paragraphs: The whole-brain image in the published figure has a 200 µm scale bar, and the synaptic insets have 10 µm bars. Giant-synapse numbers in the lateral complex rose after three days of exposure to full-spectrum light, with no learning walks required. Both scales appear in the same figure panel.

Removing ultraviolet light lowered that rise. Ants given full-spectrum light without learning walks still showed the increase. Dark controls provided the reference level for each light treatment. The experiment ran for three days before the brains were analyzed.

Central-complex volume did not follow this light-driven pattern. The light treatments were natural skylight, a filter that removed ultraviolet, and a fixed polarization pattern. Lateral-complex synapses sit along the sky-compass pathway in these ants. The lateral complex is a region of the visual pathway that the study counted synapses in.

inserts.title: Learning-walk setup defines the treatment groups
paragraphs: A table installed 30 cm above the nest entrance held the polarization filter over a 60 × 60 cm learning-walk area. Novices tested around natural nests in Greece experienced their defined skylight condition over three days. Novices performed learning walks around the nest.

A time-compensated compass has to follow the sun's position, which changes through the day. Initial learning can establish the link between those celestial changes and stable surroundings. Each treatment set how often the polarization direction changed.

Across the learning-walk schedules, volume changed in the central complex and in the mushroom-body collar, while giant-synapse counts stayed broadly similar. The continuous rotation condition changed filter orientation at 15° per hour. The natural skylight condition was one of those schedules.

inserts.title: Rotation schedules shape collar and lateral responses
paragraphs: Each of the three rotating schedules raised collar volume and the microglomerular count. A stationary pattern produced no such growth, and polarized light alone did not produce that growth either. The stationary pattern was the reference condition for the rotating schedules.

Lateral-complex giant synapses changed little across those schedules. Continuous rotation advanced the filter orientation by 15° per hour, a slower step than the hourly 45° turns, and the schedules differed in how fast the pattern rotated over three days.

Learning walks take the ant on short trips around the nest as it moves from indoor work to outdoor foraging. The sky-compass pathway runs through the lateral complex, one of the visual integration centers. Mushroom-body volume responded to the same schedules.

The coils surrounded a 60 × 60 cm platform joined to the nest, and novices learned on it for three days. The retained field pointed downward, not horizontally.

Central-complex volume rose in the natural field and in several elimination or disarray conditions over three days. Nest-directed gazes were scored from the longest pirouette pauses in each walk. Under natural conditions, those pauses point toward the nest. Those pauses were scored within each ant's own walk.

inserts.title: Ten training journeys set up two feeders
paragraphs: Ants completed ten training journeys: four to feeder A, four to B and two final journeys to A. Feeder B lay 45° to the left or right of A as viewed from the nest. Each feeder had its own channel leading from the nest during training. The nest-to-feeder channels were separated from the connecting channel.

The subsequent test removed food and opened the connecting test channel at A. At any moment, a single nest-channel entrance was open. Its distances from the nest were 4.5 m to A and 5.7 m to B. The connecting channel was new to the ants. The test then measured where the searches concentrated.

Feeder B was placed on either side of A in separate test arrangements. A shortcut links familiar destinations through a route that the ant never used during training. Feeder B's test arrangements placed it left or right of A in balanced fashion. The left and right placements were both tested.
notes: Ten training journeys set up two feeders.

paragraphs: Control ants visited feeder A alone before the test. Once food was removed, their searches centered on the old feeder and spread roughly evenly to both sides. Their distribution served as the baseline for the two-feeder searches. Without a second food source in memory, one-feeder controls show the expected search pattern.

About two-thirds of two-feeder ants turned first toward the side where the second feeder sat. The effect appeared whichever side feeder B occupied. Stored goals persist across journeys, while the current vector updates during travel.

Searches were scored as distances in metres from the start along the connecting channel. The first U-turn is an early movement, separate from the later back-and-forth searching. The searches were recorded as density distributions over the channel.

2: **Path integration** is the continual updating of direction and distance from a starting point using information gathered during movement. A **home vector** gives the direction and distance back to the nest, so it condenses the whole outward trip into one quantity. Because the update runs continuously, the animal always holds an estimate of where its nest lies.

Müller and Wehner recorded a natural foraging trip of _Cataglyphis fortis_ in Tunisia. The outward path measured 354.5 m, while the farthest point of the trip lay 113.2 m from the nest. After finding food, the ant returned along a comparatively direct inbound route. The homeward path was therefore far shorter than the path the ant had walked outward.

The gap between outward path length and nest displacement marks **vector-guided homing** rather than **route retracing**. A direct return after a winding outward route shows that the vector summed every segment of the trip into one direction and distance. A retracing ant would instead need a stored memory of every turn. The vector summary avoids that memory requirement.
3: **Passive displacement** changes an ant's position without the walking movements that normally update its **home vector**. The vector is a record of the ant's own movement, so a transfer that bypasses that movement leaves the record pointing elsewhere. A displaced ant therefore expresses a direction suited to its earlier position rather than to the nest.

Müller and Wehner tracked the course taken by individual ants after they were moved. The question was whether each ant still expressed information from its own outward movement. The nest was no longer where the earlier movements had placed it. A course that matches the outward movement would therefore reveal the origin of the heading.

The released ant's heading retained information from its outward journey despite the transfer. That result points to **movement-derived navigation** rather than immediate attraction to the true nest. The ant's heading depended on where it had been walking, not on where the nest lay. This dependence is what the displacement test was designed to reveal.
4: An **experimental path** can specify the directions and distances an ant experiences before homing. Müller and Wehner trained _Cataglyphis fortis_ through narrow plastic channels, then moved individuals to an open test field where the channels were absent. Each training path therefore defined a known sequence of directions for the ant to integrate.

The experiment varied the two legs over a range of lengths and turning angles, so many route geometries could be tested with one procedure. Release occurred soon after capture, which kept the delay between training and the directional test short. Each animal was therefore tested while its training remained recent.

The initial homeward course reflects the ant's **accumulated directional estimate** rather than its ability to follow the training channel backward. Because the channels were removed during testing, the course depends on the geometry integrated during training. The expressed direction therefore measures what the ant computed, not what it retraced. This measure therefore isolates the integrated estimate.
5: **Systematic error** is a directional deviation that varies predictably with an experimental manipulation, in contrast with random scatter among journeys. Müller and Wehner measured the angular difference between the true homeward direction and the course expressed after two-leg training. The sign of each deviation shows which way the expressed course lay.

With outbound legs of 10 m and 5 m, the error grew as the turning angle approached about 150°, reaching roughly 20° in the published measurements. The error fell back toward zero in the straight and reversed arrangements. The largest bias therefore appeared at intermediate angles rather than at the extremes.

The angle-dependent pattern supports an **approximate updating rule** for the _Cataglyphis_ trajectories tested. The rule is written as a mathematical account, so it can be checked against route geometries that the original experiments did not use. The rule makes quantitative predictions for these geometries. It can therefore be tested on new route geometries.
6: A **celestial compass** derives heading information from features of the sky. Direct sunlight and the pattern of **polarized skylight** provide related but separable information. Polarization refers to the orientation of the electric field oscillation in a light wave. Ants can therefore draw heading information from either source. Both sources therefore contribute heading information.

Müller and Wehner measured homing errors while the ants used the sun, polarized skylight, or both. Each compass condition was tested with the same navigation procedure. The compass input was the only variable that changed between conditions. The homing error therefore reflects the compass information available to the ant. The sun and polarized skylight were tested separately and together.

Because the error pattern persisted across compass conditions, the bias lies in the path-integration computation rather than in one defective sky cue. A single sky cue would have produced a pattern tied to that cue alone. The persistence therefore points to the computation itself. The bias therefore has a computational origin.
7: An explanation fitted to one route geometry has to predict a different sequence of movements. Müller and Wehner added a third leg to the channel arrangement, introducing a second 90° turn in place of repeating the original two-leg design. The new route tested whether the rule still held for an unfamiliar sequence of turns.

Released ants deviated by 30.8° from the true home direction, and the approximation derived from the earlier experiments predicted a deviation of 33.7°. This close agreement shows that the rule generalizes beyond the angles used to derive it. The rule predicted that value before the three-leg test. This match is an independent test of the approximation.

The experiment measured the animal's course rather than the voltage, transmitter or synaptic activity of an identified integrator. The behavioral match therefore describes the output of the computation rather than its cellular mechanism. The result constrains the computation rather than identifying its cells. Cellular recordings would be needed to test that mechanism.
8: Route geometry determines how an approximate path integrator accumulates error. A sharp sustained turn can produce a large deviation, whereas turns in opposite directions can partly cancel their effects on the estimated homeward direction. Opposing turns keep the accumulated error small along many natural routes. Repeated sharp reversals produce the largest errors.

Müller and Wehner tested the proposed updating rule against recorded natural foraging paths. In the displaced example, the expressed course departed from the real nest direction by about 20°, matching the direction predicted from that ant's outward trajectory. The approximation was tested on paths that the ants had really walked.

The authors observed that natural _Cataglyphis_ paths seldom contain the repeated sharp backward turns that generate the largest experimental errors. Under this ecological interpretation, the home vector serves typical routes well. Repeated sharp reversals produce the largest errors, so natural routes rarely expose the rule's weakest case. The authors' argument rests on the route statistics of natural foraging.
9: An **odometer** is a mechanism for estimating distance traveled. A **stride** is one complete movement cycle of a particular leg.
